stories.title: Trump admin considers more semiconductor tariffs, could include data center servers
stories.summary: The Trump administration is weighing additional semiconductor tariffs that could extend to data center servers, according to reports.
stories.why_it_matters: Tariffs reaching servers would raise the cost of AI infrastructure buildouts in the US and ripple through Asian supply chains where most of the hardware is manufactured and assembled. APAC operators and suppliers could see both cost pressure on exports and shifted demand as buyers reconsider sourcing and deployment geographies.
stories.content:
The Trump administration is considering further tariffs on semiconductors.

Such tariffs may even be expanded, Politico reports, to include the goods that use chips - including data center servers. Tariffs are paid by the importer, not the exporter.

![money_dollar_bills_benjamin_franklin_1366x768_2.original.jpg](https://media.datacenterdynamics.com/media/images/money_dollar_bills_benjamin_franklin_1366x768_.width-358_JqglF12.jpg) 

The tariff discussions are still in an early stage, and could change in the coming weeks or months. As it stands, the administration is considering a phase-in period for the new tariffs, while Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is in favor of using it to force investment in US chip manufacturing. Those that invest would escape the tariffs.

“Reshoring semiconductor manufacturing is a top priority for President Trump, whose policies have already secured hundreds of billions of dollars of investments in this key sector,” White House spokesperson Kush Desai said of the report.

“The Trump administration remains focused on delivering more investments and economic relief for the American people while safeguarding our national security.”

Tariffs could cost the US about $90 billion in GDP losses annually and delay or cancel around 20 percent of data center projects planned through 2030, the Computer and Communications Industry Association (CCIA) claimed in June.

stories.title: NVIDIA Expands NVLink Fusion with New NVHBM Memory
stories.summary: NVIDIA has expanded its NVLink Fusion ecosystem with NVHBM memory, decoupling high-bandwidth memory control from the chip itself and opening the technology to multiple suppliers. The move could give cloud builders additional compute headroom and more flexibility in system design.
stories.why_it_matters: Opening NVHBM to multiple vendors loosens one of the tightest chokepoints in AI hardware supply, potentially easing the memory bottlenecks that have constrained GPU deployments. For hyperscalers and OEMs, it promises more design freedom — while also deepening their integration into NVIDIA's interconnect ecosystem.
stories.content:
![NVIDIA expands NVLink Fusion with new NVHBM memory](https://datacenternews.asia/uploads/story/2026/08/28/neutral-hyperscale-data-center-server-racks-gpu-board-digital-illustration-story-317813.webp) 

![Sean Mitchell](https://datacenternews.asia/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyOSwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--a929a91c2a04d9af95ed98b14ed4d405bc70c1a7/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/IMG_3092.webp) 

NVIDIA has expanded NVLink Fusion with a new high-bandwidth memory technology called NVHBM, extending its semi-custom AI infrastructure offering into memory design.

NVHBM moves the memory controller from the XPU die into the HBM base die, changing the long-established arrangement in which the controller sits on the processor itself. NVIDIA says that shift can free more silicon area for compute while improving memory throughput and reducing power use.

The technology is based on the same approach NVIDIA plans to use in future GPUs. It will be validated and supplied by multiple memory partners, with the aim of giving NVLink Fusion customers a standard implementation that can be sourced from more than one provider.

According to NVIDIA, the design delivers up to 30% greater memory bandwidth and 15% lower HBM power consumption than standard HBM4E. It can also free up to 25% more area on the XPU compute die by removing the memory controller from that chip.

### AWS link

Amazon's Annapurna Labs will be the first group to work on NVHBM under its broader collaboration with NVIDIA on NVLink Fusion. The work will also cover the NVLink scale-up architecture for AI workloads.

Annapurna Labs is already part of Amazon's Trainium effort, and support for NVLink Fusion is planned for the next generation of those chips, starting with Trainium4. That would allow Amazon chips and NVIDIA GPUs to operate together within a shared rack-scale architecture.

"NVHBM represents a new architectural approach to advancing high-bandwidth memory performance and efficiency," said Nafea Bshara, Vice President of Annapurna Labs at Amazon.

"We look forward to this technology collaboration to benefit future AWS infrastructure designs," Bshara said.

### Memory shift

High-bandwidth memory has become central to AI system design as model sizes grow and data movement puts more strain on system architecture. In conventional designs, memory controllers occupy space on the XPU die, limiting how much of that silicon is available for compute functions.

NVIDIA's proposal is to embed its custom memory controller in the three-dimensional HBM stack instead. That should reduce the engineering work needed to integrate and qualify memory from different suppliers because the NVHBM implementation will be standardised across several providers.

That matters for cloud companies and chip designers seeking more customised AI systems without having to build every element themselves. NVLink Fusion is NVIDIA's framework for linking custom XPUs and CPUs to its broader rack-scale platform, including chiplets, interconnect, switches, systems and racks.

### Broader strategy

The move shows how NVIDIA is trying to extend its influence beyond GPUs into the surrounding architecture of AI data centres. Rather than offering only finished processors, it is packaging interconnect, system design and now memory architecture into a platform that outside partners can use with their own silicon.

For hyperscalers and AI-focused infrastructure developers, that model offers a route to building semi-custom systems while staying aligned with NVIDIA's networking and rack design. It also gives NVIDIA a way to remain at the centre of AI infrastructure decisions even when customers develop chips in-house.

NVLink Fusion gives partners access to NVIDIA NVLink chiplets, NVLink-C2C, NVLink switches, and MGX systems and racks, alongside a wider ecosystem of CPU partners, ASIC designers, system manufacturers, and other technology providers. NVIDIA positions the platform as a way for customers to focus on XPU design while relying on an existing stack for scale-up and scale-out networking, rack systems, and software.

Adding memory architecture strengthens that proposition, particularly as AI customers look for gains not just from processor performance but from the balance between compute, memory and system efficiency. As AI agents and very large models place heavier demands on infrastructure, control over those design trade-offs is becoming more important across the supply chain.

Amazon's participation gives the effort an early high-profile user with a history of building its own AI silicon.

stories.title: AWS, NVIDIA to Deploy 2 Million More GPUs for AI Workloads
stories.summary: AWS plans to add two million NVIDIA GPUs to its infrastructure to keep pace with demand for AI computing. The expansion deepens the cloud provider's dependence on NVIDIA silicon, including its robotics-related platforms.
stories.why_it_matters: A deployment of this scale locks in enormous power, space, and supply-chain commitments, tightening GPU availability for smaller buyers and reinforcing NVIDIA's grip on cloud AI infrastructure. For data center operators and utilities, it translates into sustained pressure on capacity pipelines for years to come.
stories.content:
![AWS, NVIDIA to deploy 2 million more GPUs for AI workloads](https://datacenternews.asia/uploads/story/2026/08/28/installation-cloud-data-center-robotic-arms-gpu-chip-digital-illustration-story-317818.webp) 

# AWS, NVIDIA to deploy 2 million more GPUs for AI workloads

Fri, 28th Aug 2026
![Mark Tarre](https://datacenternews.asia/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyMywicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--47487b3f4571870114142b0dc77b848fa071f6b5/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/MARK%20TARRE%20TECHDAY%20PORTRAIT.webp) 

Amazon Web Services and NVIDIA will deploy 2 million additional graphics processing units for artificial intelligence workloads and expand their collaboration into central processing units, networking and robotics.

The move further scales infrastructure tied to surging demand for AI computing, as cloud providers and chipmakers race to add processing capacity for model training and deployment.

The deployment will add to the large installed base of NVIDIA hardware already used across AWS's cloud platform. NVIDIA has become the dominant supplier of AI chips, while AWS has sought to balance demand for NVIDIA systems with its own in-house silicon, including Trainium and Inferentia.

### Wider build-out

The broader tie-up points to a relationship that now extends beyond graphics processors. By naming CPUs, networking and robotics alongside GPUs, the companies signalled that they are working across a wider set of technologies at the centre of data centre expansion and AI system design.

Cloud infrastructure groups have been spending heavily to secure enough processors, networking equipment and power to keep pace with corporate and consumer use of generative AI services. NVIDIA's chips remain central to that build-out because they are widely used to train large language models and run inference tasks after deployment.

For AWS, the additional GPUs could help it serve customers that want access to NVIDIA systems through the cloud rather than build their own data centre estates. The arrangement also reflects how large cloud operators are trying to preserve flexibility by combining merchant chip supply with internally developed processors and tightly integrated networking gear.

Robotics is a newer area of overlap. NVIDIA has pushed software and hardware platforms for robotic systems and industrial automation, while Amazon has long invested in warehouse automation and machine learning systems in its logistics network. A deeper collaboration in that segment suggests the partnership could extend beyond cloud computing into physical AI applications.

### Competitive pressure

The announcement comes as competition intensifies among hyperscale cloud providers to secure the equipment needed for AI services. Microsoft, Google and other large operators have been expanding their infrastructure footprints, signing supply agreements and introducing their own chip designs in an effort to reduce costs and manage dependence on external vendors.

That backdrop has increased NVIDIA's strategic importance to the biggest technology groups. Even as customers pursue alternatives, its GPUs and networking products remain deeply embedded in AI system architecture, making access to supply a priority for cloud operators serving start-ups, developers and large corporate clients.

The inclusion of CPUs in the expanded alliance is also notable because it suggests closer alignment in how AI systems are assembled. While GPUs do most of the heavy lifting for many AI tasks, CPUs remain essential for orchestrating workloads, managing memory and running broader application environments inside data centres.

Networking has become equally important as AI clusters grow larger. Moving data quickly between processors is critical to training advanced models efficiently, and NVIDIA has expanded in that segment through high-speed interconnect and data centre networking products. Closer work with AWS on networking could therefore shape how future AI clusters are configured within the cloud provider's infrastructure.

### Industry context

The scale of 2 million additional GPUs underlines how AI has become a capital-intensive contest among the world's largest technology companies. Building and operating systems at that size requires substantial investment not only in chips, but also in servers, networking, software integration, cooling and electricity.

Investors and customers have been watching whether spending on AI infrastructure will translate into sustainable revenue growth for cloud providers and semiconductor groups. AWS has been under pressure to show that demand for AI services can support the cost of rapid expansion, while NVIDIA has faced questions about how long the current level of demand can continue.

Even so, the latest deployment shows that both companies are still preparing for further growth in AI use across business software, consumer applications and industrial systems. The addition of 2 million GPUs, alongside broader work in CPUs, networking and robotics, points to a partnership becoming more deeply woven into the infrastructure behind the current AI market.

NVIDIA is the dominant supplier of AI chips, while AWS remains one of the world's largest cloud operators seeking to meet rising customer demand for access to advanced computing systems.

stories.title: X2M sets up dedicated data center subsidiary and signs a deal for data center project
stories.summary: As Australian IoT company moves into the data center sphere
stories.content:
Australian IoT company X2M Connect has established a dedicated data center subsidiary as it moves into the data center sphere.

The wholly owned subsidiary, named X2MDC, has been formed to contract and deliver high-density GPU-accelerated data centers. X2M’s planned pipeline of data center projects could reach up to 150MW.

X2MDC operations will include commissioning, engineering, design, delivery, installation, and operation of data centers. It will also provide Software as a Service (SaaS) throughout the operating life of the facilities.

The subsidiary will provide two services: Platform Services, which consist of AI integration and management for data centers by bringing cooling, power, water, and environmental systems, and Managed Delivery, the end-to-end service from contracting to delivering a complete data center, including design, supplier selection, and long-term operations.

The company says it expects contracts to vary depending on customer requirements.

X2M CEO Mohan Jesudason said: “X2MDC gives us a dedicated vehicle to execute on our pipeline of possible data center opportunities. X2M has spent more than a decade connecting and optimizing devices across water, gas and energy, and that is exactly the challenge for every AI facility being planned or built today.”

He added: “We are excited at the prospect of delivering services in association with some of the top providers in the world and offering a comprehensive platform and delivery service to land and data center owners across the country."

The formation of X2M’s dedicated data center subsidiary business follows a McKinsey report published in April 2026, which indicates an increase in Australian data center demand from 1.5GW in 2025 to as much as 5GW by 2030, which the management consulting firm expects will require up to AU$190bn (~US$135bn) of digital infrastructure investment.

## **X2M signs a deal for an AI-enabled data center project**

X2M signed a binding agreement to deliver an AI-enabled data center this week, just two days after forming its dedicated data center subsidiary.

The company has been contracted to provide a high-density GPU data center with an estimated project cost of more than AU$250m (~US$180m), with full delivery over a three-to-five-year period.

![X2M Connect logo](https://media.datacenterdynamics.com/media/images/Screenshot_2026-08-28_124441.width-358.png) 

The customer is yet to be named and the location yet to be confirmed, and the company has said the agreement does not currently include a value for the data center power capacity to be deployed.

The customer contract is the first of X2M’s dedicated data center subsidiary business and will operate under the company’s Managed Delivery business model. It will consequently include the provision of services for engineering, design, supply, installation, commissioning, and operation of the data center.

Within the agreement, X2M is pre-approved to contract partners across telecommunications, energy systems, compute, AI chip, networking, and research. The agreement is conditional only on approval being given for the development of the data center.

Jesudason shared: “This agreement is transformational for X2M. We play a key role in the data center delivery, and that in turn creates a materially large business opportunity for us. We are excited at the prospect of delivering services from some of the top providers in the world and offering a comprehensive service to this customer and land and data center owners across the country.”

The contracted data center is part of X2M’s pipeline of potential Australian data centers, the majority of which will be located in Queensland. In some locations, facility development has already been approved. The data centers will range in size from 1MW upwards, with a target total of 150MW across the company’s pipeline of potential data center sites.

Australia-based X2M was founded in 2019 and is headquartered in Mount Waverley, Victoria, Australia. The company describes itself as a smart city technology company that delivers solutions to enhance productivity, reduce operational costs, and improve public safety for utility and government customers. The firm claims to have connected more than 500,000 devices supporting more than 90 customers across five geographic regions, and continues to expand its footprint.

In June this year, X2M announced a partnership with real estate firm Resi Ventures to develop data centers across regional Australia. The collaboration shared that it had completed settlement for land approximately 10 kilometers (6.2 miles) from Ballarat’s central business district in Victoria in July. Allegedly, the data center will be a high-density AI-enabled facility, with a potential capacity ranging from 10-100MW.

stories.title: Nvidia pauses some cloud revenue sharing deals - report
stories.summary: NVIDIA has reportedly paused some of its cloud revenue-sharing arrangements over concerns the structures could attract antitrust scrutiny.
stories.why_it_matters: Pulling back from revenue-sharing suggests NVIDIA sees regulatory risk in deals that tie its financing and chip dominance ever closer to cloud customers. If the pause becomes permanent, it could chill the creative deal-making that has financed much of the AI capacity expansion and invite closer examination of similar arrangements elsewhere.
stories.content:
Nvidia is pausing some of its cloud revenue-sharing deals, in which it partners with cloud providers to set up AI compute clusters.

According to a report from Wall Street Journal and citing people familiar with the matter, the company has halted some of these initiatives over concerns that it could lease to antitrust scrutiny.

![Nvidia](https://media.datacenterdynamics.com/media/images/Nvidia_wk6Y1B5.width-358.jpg) 

Nvidia announced plans for the revenue-sharing agreements in July 2026, in which the chip designer acts as a financial backstop for companies seeking to deploy large-scale clusters, in return for part of the revenue from operations.

The backstop also sees Nvidia agreeing to rent back unused GPUs at a fixed rate. Firmus and Sharon AI were among the first companies to have adopted the offer, with Firmus deploying 170,000 GPUs in Batam, Indonesia, and Sharon AI deploying 40,000 GB300 GPUs.

According to WSJ, this is merely a pause on such deals, and the program has not been fully scrapped.

Despite this, Nvidia told *DCD:* "The new business model we introduced in July that opens up compute access to the fast-growing AI ecosystem is still in place and continues to evolve due to high demand.” 

These reports emerged shortly after Nvidia posted its Q2 earnings, in which it saw revenue of $96.2bn, up 18 percent from the previous quarter and up 106 percent from a year ago, while GAAP and non-GAAP gross margins were both 75 percent.

Notably, the earnings also showed that Nvidia disclosed $108.5 billion in guarantees and other agreements to enable AI cloud computing. $3.5bn was for land, power, and shell guarantees for AI clouds, while $105bn was toward SB Energy Corp for OpenAI's Ohio campus.

stories.title: Indosat's Infra Fiber Teknologi spin-off launches AI-ready RAIA Grid
stories.summary: Infra Fiber Teknologi, a spin-off from Indonesian telco Indosat, has launched RAIA Grid, an AI-ready infrastructure platform that embeds machine learning, AI, and agentic AI capabilities into its fiber network operations.
stories.why_it_matters: The launch shows Indonesian telecom infrastructure players moving up the value chain, monetizing fiber assets with AI-driven services rather than competing on connectivity alone. If the model gains traction, it could accelerate AI-ready network investment across Southeast Asia's underserved markets and reshape how regional telcos structure their infrastructure businesses.
stories.content:
Infra Fiber Teknologi (IFT), the digital infrastructure spin-off of Indosat Ooredoo Hutchison, has announced the launch of an AI-powered digital infrastructure platform.

Dubbed "RAIA Grid," the platform aims to establish Indonesia's "digital highway."

![RAIA Grid (1)](https://media.datacenterdynamics.com/media/images/RAIA_Grid_1.width-358.jpg) 

It comes after Indonesian telco Indosat spun off its fiber business last month to create IFT as an independent fiber infrastructure platform along with Indonesian investment firm Arsari Group.

The company operates more than 86,000km (53,437 miles) of fiber infrastructure across Indonesia. This is made up of backbone, domestic subsea, and access networks, as an independently governed, open-access platform.

IFT will leverage its existing infrastructure as part of its RAIA Grid project.

IFT's RAIA Grid will embed Machine Learning (ML), Artificial Intelligence (AI), and Agentic AI into how its infrastructure is planned, deployed, and operated, which the company notes makes it "an AI-powered infrastructure platform by design."

These features will enable the company to "support intelligent network planning and demand forecasting, optimize fiber routes and investment decisions, accelerate deployment through automation, and enable predictive maintenance and more autonomous network operations."

According to IFT, its RAIA Grid platform is designed to support connectivity for 5G, fiber-to-the-home (FTTH), and data center-to-data center (DC-to-DC) connections.

RAIA Grid is an open-access model that will serve telcos, data centers, cloud providers, hyperscalers, and enterprises to create infrastructure pathways that allow data and digital services to move efficiently across the country.

“RAIA Grid is built with a clear strategic ambition: to become the digital superhighway connecting Indonesia’s increasingly complex digital ecosystem, from data center to data center, and ultimately connecting Indonesia to the world," said Hendri Mulya Syam, president director of RAIA Grid.

"We are creating the infrastructure layer that enables compute, data and intelligence to move seamlessly at scale, turning connectivity into a strategic advantage for Indonesia’s digital future.”

Vikram Sinha, CEO, Indosat, added that the RAIA Grid project ties into the company's Zankore by Indosat data center play, which was announced last month.

The carrier has paired with the wider Ooredoo Group, Nokia, and Nvidia to launch Zankore by Indosat as it aims to deploy up to 1GW of AI data center capacity.

“The opportunity ahead is bigger than connectivity. RAIA Grid is building the highway that connects data centers, cloud platforms, businesses and AI infrastructure, creating the foundation for a full AI stack," said Sinha.

"By bringing together RAIA Grid, Indosat and Zankore, we are connecting the critical layers needed to make AI more real, scalable, and accessible across Indonesia. This convergence allows us to move beyond connecting infrastructure to connecting intelligence, creating new opportunities for businesses, industries, and people.”

Aryo Djojohadikusumo, deputy CEO and COO of Arsari Group, added: "Our ambition is to build the capabilities Indonesia will need for the next era of computing and AI. We are looking beyond connectivity to support high-performance computing today, while laying the foundation for future capabilities, including supercomputer manufacturing in Indonesia. By building these capabilities here, we can strengthen Indonesia’s technological independence and create opportunities to compete on a global stage.”

stories.title: Alibaba Cloud launches its first cloud region in Brazil
stories.summary: Alibaba Cloud, the AI infrastructure and intelligence backbone of Alibaba Group, has announced the launch of its first cloud region in Brazil, giving South American enterprises, startups, developers, and public institutions direct access to a full portfolio of cloud services running on local infrastructure. The region will offer a comprehensive suite of cloud computing products […]
stories.content:
Alibaba Cloud, the Alibaba Group’s global AI infrastructure provider, has launched its first cloud region in Brazil, consisting of two data centers.

The new region offers businesses, startups, developers, and public institutions access to a comprehensive portfolio of cloud services with local infrastructure, designed for mission-critical workloads that require low latency, resilience, and data governance. The company also plans to introduce enterprise-grade agent-based AI services in the region.

The launch marks Alibaba Cloud’s first region in South America and expands its presence in Latin America, following the inauguration of the Mexico region in February 2025. With this expansion, the company now operates 106 availability zones across 31 regions worldwide, as part of a global investment of $53 billion (275.4 billion reais) in artificial intelligence infrastructure.

Allen Guo, general manager of the Latin America Region and vice president of International Business at Alibaba Cloud Intelligence, highlighted Brazil as one of the world’s most dynamic digital economies and as a key market for the company’s expansion in the region. According to Guo, the combination of local infrastructure, an AI and cloud portfolio, and a growing partner ecosystem aims to support Brazilian companies in developing cloud and AI capabilities, connecting them to the company’s global network.

The new region offers services ranging from computing, storage, and networking to databases, big data, and cloud-native solutions, enabling local customers to operate with greater availability, stability, and disaster recovery, in compliance with local cybersecurity and data governance regulations and standards. To meet the demand for AI, the company also plans to launch a suite of enterprise agent services in Brazil—including ACS Agent Sandbox, DAS Agent, Data Agent for Analytics, Meta Agent, DataWorks Data Agent, STAROps, NAPal, Agent Security Center, AI Security Guardrails 2.0, and Agentic SOC—designed for the development, operation, and protection of AI agents at scale.

Alibaba Cloud has also established local partnerships to strengthen its ecosystem in the country. Insi, a Brazilian provider of technology solutions, will use Alibaba’s cloud and AI portfolio to offer customized solutions to corporate clients. Roberto Certo, chief revenue officer at Insi, stated that the new local region enables the company to serve businesses undergoing modernization with the necessary performance, security, and data residency.

Meanwhile, 4Linux, a Brazilian company specializing in open source and IT services, will combine Alibaba Cloud’s Qwen models with its expertise in deployment and training to bring generative AI to companies in the country. According to Marcelo Marques, co-founder of 4Linux, the partnership offers customers a reliable foundation for building and scaling AI solutions, supported by Alibaba Cloud’s technological leadership and commitment to its partners.

The announcement comes amid recent advances by Alibaba in open-source models, such as Qwen3.8-Flash and Qwen3.8-27B, in addition to the release of open model weights for Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B—the most powerful model in the Qwen line to date. The launch in Brazil continues Alibaba Cloud’s regional expansion, which already includes operations in Mexico, France, Japan, South Korea, and Malaysia.

stories.title: Nscale Secures $45 Billion AI Compute Contract, Anthropic Reportedly Customer
stories.summary: Nscale has reportedly secured a six-year, $45 billion contract for artificial intelligence (AI) compute capacity at its Monarch campus in West Virginia, with Reuters identifying Anthropic as the customer. This commitment provides Nscale with a major anchor tenant for its 1.35GW AI compute facility ahead of a potential US initial public offering (IPO).
stories.content:
Nscale has reportedly secured a six-year, $45 billion contract for artificial intelligence (AI) compute capacity at its Monarch campus in West Virginia, with Reuters identifying Anthropic as the customer. This commitment provides Nscale with a major anchor tenant for its 1.35GW AI compute facility ahead of a potential US initial public offering (IPO).

Highlights

Nscale secured a $45 billion contract for AI compute capacity at its West Virginia Monarch campus.

Reuters reports Anthropic is the customer for the six-year, 460MW deal, involving Nvidia Vera Rubin systems.

The agreement accounts for about one-third of Monarch's initial 1.35GW AI compute capacity.

Microsoft reportedly withdrew from an earlier letter of intent for capacity at the Monarch campus.

Nscale expects capacity to be available in late 2027, ahead of a potential US IPO.

Nscale has secured a substantial $45 billion contract for AI compute capacity at its Monarch campus in West Virginia, according to a regulatory announcement from Aker, which identifies Nscale as its second-largest portfolio holding. Reuters, citing a person familiar with the matter, has reported that Anthropic is the customer behind this six-year agreement.The deal is understood to cover approximately 460MW of compute capacity and will involve Nvidia’s forthcoming Vera Rubin systems. This commitment positions Nscale with a significant anchor customer for its Monarch campus as the British AI infrastructure company prepares for a possible US stock-market listing.

Monarch Campus Capacity and Deployment

Nscale’s first phase at the West Virginia site is designed to provide 1.35GW of AI compute capacity. The reported Anthropic agreement would account for roughly one-third of this initial development, with Anthropic expected to occupy the first of three planned buildings.The capacity is anticipated to become available in late 2027, aligning with the previously outlined timetable for Monarch’s initial deployments. This deal also reconfigures earlier plans, as Bloomberg reported that Microsoft had withdrawn from a letter of intent signed in March, which covered up to 1.35GW at the campus and around 430,000 Nvidia Vera Rubin graphics processing units (GPUs).

Anthropic's Growing Compute Demand

Anthropic has increasingly prioritised securing additional compute resources. Earlier this year, the company introduced tighter usage limits for some of its Claude services due to rising demand. Subsequently, a separate agreement for over 300MW of SpaceX compute capacity allowed these limits to be increased again.

IPO Preparations Underway

The agreement between Anthropic and Nscale comes shortly after reports indicated that Nscale could seek to raise up to $3 billion through a US IPO, potentially as early as September. Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan are reportedly involved in the potential offering. Prospective investors have been informed that Nscale possesses approximately $51 billion in contracted revenue, though it is unclear if this figure includes the new deal with Anthropic.

stories.title: Armada Launches 10 MW Orion Modular Data Center for Sovereign AI
stories.summary: Modular AI infrastructure developer Armada has launched Orion, a 10 MW prefabricated data center designed for rapid deployment within existing structures. This development aims to support sovereign AI initiatives by providing scalable, high-density compute capacity.
stories.content:
Modular AI infrastructure developer Armada has launched Orion, a 10 MW prefabricated data center designed for rapid deployment within existing structures. This development aims to support sovereign AI initiatives by providing scalable, high-density compute capacity.

Highlights

Armada launched Orion, a 10 MW prefabricated data center for AI infrastructure.

Fossefall selected Armada to help build 1 GW of Nordic-owned AI capacity by 2030.

Orion supports 2,880 GPUs across 40 racks, compatible with NVIDIA Blackwell.

Modular data center market is valued at US$34 billion, projected to reach US$75.77 billion by 2030.

Armada, a developer of modular artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure, has introduced Orion, a 10 megawatt (MW) prefabricated data center. This new unit is designed for deployment within existing structures, offering a solution for rapid AI infrastructure buildouts.The company has also been selected by Fossefall as a technology partner for its initiative to establish 1 gigawatt (GW) of Nordic-owned AI capacity by 2030. As part of this partnership, Armada will supply Fossefall with five Leviathan Galleons, each supporting a maximum of 1.77 MW of IT load.

Orion’s Capacity and Design

Orion is engineered to scale to hundreds of megawatts across distributed sites. Each unit integrates compute, networking, power, and cooling into a prefabricated six-module core. The system supports 2,880 graphics processing units (GPUs) across 40 racks and is compatible with NVIDIA Blackwell architecture, while also being Vera Rubin-ready. The units are designed to achieve N+1 redundancy.Dan Wright, Armada Co-founder and Chief Executive Officer, stated, "AI infrastructure should be fast to deploy, easy to scale, and sovereign wherever it needs to live. Orion raises the ceiling on what a single deployment can deliver " ten megawatts per unit, infinitely scalable, in months instead of years."Øyvind Vesterdal, Fossefall Chief Executive Officer, commented on the partnership, "We selected Armada for its best-in-class technology, proven execution capabilities, and ability to significantly accelerate time to market. We were also keen to work with a strategic partner manufacturing in Europe, to provide a resilient supply chain and reduce exposure to global disruptions."

Modular Data Center Market Trend

The modular data center market is currently valued at an estimated US$34 billion, according to Grand View Research. Projections indicate a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 17.4% through 2030, with the market expected to reach US$75.77 billion. This growth is driven by increasing demand for compute capacity closer to the edge and the pursuit of sovereign AI capabilities.

AI workloads are pushing rack power densities from 132 kW towards 1 MW, redefining resilience needs.

The escalating power requirements driven by artificial intelligence (AI) workloads are fundamentally reshaping how data centres approach battery infrastructure, moving beyond simple backup to strategic energy management for resilience, flexibility, and sustainability.Racks drawing 132 kW today are projected to push towards 1 MW in the near future, compelling a re-evaluation of data centre resilience strategies. Cooling systems, which can no longer rely solely on thermal ride-through, now require uninterrupted power supply (UPS) systems to safeguard pumps, cooling distribution units (CDUs), and control mechanisms, alongside traditional IT loads. This convergence is transforming cooling and power into an integrated design challenge.

Grid Constraints and Demand Shifts

The UK’s grid connection queue, currently exceeding 700 GW against an available 81 GW, underscores the global challenge of securing adequate power. AI is not only increasing overall electricity consumption but also altering the nature of demand, with large graphics processing unit (GPU) clusters experiencing rapid ramp-up and ramp-down cycles. This dynamic demand profile necessitates a more strategic role for batteries.Batteries are evolving from passive backup components into active energy assets. This enables them to support critical functions such as peak shaving, optimising renewable energy consumption, and, where commercially viable, providing grid-balancing and flexibility services.

Battery Technology Evolution and Strategy

Current battery solutions predominantly include Valve Regulated Lead Acid (VRLA) and lithium-ion technologies. However, emerging options such as sodium-ion, flow batteries, and second-life electric vehicle (EV) batteries are being explored for their potential roles in data centre power infrastructure.Paul Lowbridge, General Sales Manager – Reserve & Renewable Power at GS Yuasa Battery Sales UK Ltd, emphasised that resilience in the AI era begins well before a power outage. He highlighted the importance of selecting the appropriate battery chemistry, integrating intelligent monitoring with proactive maintenance, and adopting a comprehensive whole-lifecycle approach to battery management.

stories.title: Singapore Launches Liquid Cooling Standard for Tropical Data Centers
stories.summary: Singapore has published what it describes as the world's first national standard for liquid cooling in tropical data centers, targeting the high-density racks demanded by AI workloads. The standard addresses region-specific challenges such as equipment corrosion and reliability in hot, humid conditions.
stories.why_it_matters: A formal standard lowers the adoption risk for operators considering liquid cooling in Southeast Asia's punishing climate, potentially accelerating retrofits and new-build designs across the region. Other tropical markets may follow Singapore's lead, making this a template for how regulators push energy efficiency as AI densities climb.
stories.content:
- **Liquid cooling can cut data-centre energy use by over 30%.**

Singapore has introduced what the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) and Enterprise Singapore (EnterpriseSG) describe as the world’s first liquid-cooling standard for tropical data centres. The standard addresses facilities supporting high-density computing equipment used for AI and other advanced workloads.

The Singapore Standard SS 726:2026, titled *Liquid Cooling in Tropical Data Centres*, was developed by IMDA and EnterpriseSG through the Singapore Standards Council. The standard covers the planning, design, deployment, operation, maintenance, and risk management of liquid-cooled systems.

Its foreword links the move toward liquid cooling with higher rack densities, noting that the data-centre industry is shifting from low-density to high-density racks with different infrastructure, space-planning, and operational requirements from conventional air-cooled systems. SS 726 also states that traditional air-cooling designs become less efficient as IT equipment increases in density and energy use. It builds on existing international liquid-cooling specifications while adding requirements and recommendations for systems operating under tropical temperatures and humidity.

### AI racks push power higher

Newer AI systems illustrate the amount of power that can now be concentrated within a single rack. Nvidia’s DGX GB200 NVL72, for example, combines 72 Blackwell GPUs and 36 Grace CPUs in one rack-scale system and has an approximate rack power consumption of 120kW.

The system uses liquid cooling for its CPUs and GPUs, while components including networking and storage equipment remain air cooled. Liquid runs through manifolds and cold plates attached to the processors.

SS 726 addresses heat removal at the data-centre level, covering systems that use coolant to remove heat directly from components such as CPUs, GPUs, and tensor processing units. The standard does not cover rear-door systems that use liquid to remove heat from air behind equipment racks or other indirect liquid-cooling designs. Two-phase and hybrid single- and two-phase cooling systems are also outside its scope.

According to SS 726, removing heat directly from heat-generating components can maintain lower and more stable operating temperatures than air cooling at comparable rack densities. It can also reduce server-fan power consumption and the risk of thermal throttling, where processors reduce performance as operating temperatures rise. A greater share of heat removed by liquid can also support denser equipment deployments while reducing residual heat released into the data hall.

IMDA and EnterpriseSG said liquid cooling can reduce energy consumption at the data-centre level by more than 30% compared with traditional air cooling.

### Cooling for tropical conditions

Singapore’s tropical climate adds specific requirements to data-centre cooling design. SS 726 identifies high humidity and ambient temperatures that often exceed 30°C as conditions that require additional operational measures.

Cooling already represents a large part of data-centre energy use. IMDA has previously estimated that cooling systems can account for up to 40% of total energy consumption in a typical data centre, with warmer tropical conditions requiring additional energy to operate cooling systems.

Singapore’s earlier Tropical Data Centre Standard allows facilities to operate safely at higher temperatures. IMDA said each 1°C increase in data-centre operating temperature can produce cooling-energy savings of around 2% to 5%.

SS 726 covers systems that remove heat directly from increasingly dense IT equipment. The standard states that liquid-cooling systems designed for fluid temperatures above 40°C are suited to tropical environments because they can use higher coolant temperatures for heat rejection.

This can reduce reliance on energy-intensive chillers, according to the standard. Higher-temperature liquid also carries waste heat at a higher temperature than conventional hot-air recapture, which can make the recovered heat more suitable for reuse where practical.

Tropical conditions also introduce specific operational risks. IMDA and EnterpriseSG said high temperatures and humidity can contribute to equipment corrosion, which can affect cooling efficiency and system reliability.

Installing liquid-cooled computing equipment requires supporting infrastructure beyond the processors themselves. SS 726 covers liquid-cooling facilities and equipment, pre-deployment testing and commissioning, operations and maintenance, risk management, and sustainability indicators.

The standard includes different coolant distribution unit, or CDU, configurations, including rack-mounted systems and floor-mounted liquid-to-liquid and liquid-to-air units. CDUs connect computing equipment with the wider cooling infrastructure and manage the flow of coolant through the system.

Liquid-cooled AI systems also require monitoring for coolant leaks and other cooling-system faults. Nvidia’s DGX GB systems, for example, incorporate leak detection to identify leaks before they damage equipment.

SS 726 provides guidance on cooling fluids, materials, maintenance, and other operational risks. It also supports the integration of liquid cooling with existing air-cooled data centres, covering facilities that use both cooling methods.

SS 726 also includes recommendations for measuring and optimising water use associated with liquid-cooling infrastructure.

IMDA and EnterpriseSG developed the standard with input from industry, academia, and technical experts.

“Liquid cooling is increasingly important to support the higher power densities required for AI and other advanced computing workloads, while improving cooling efficiency,” Aileen Chia, deputy chief executive at IMDA, said.

### Singapore adds data-centre capacity

Singapore has also provisionally allocated 200MW of new data-centre capacity to four operators under its second Data Centre Call for Application. IMDA and the Singapore Economic Development Board announced the allocations on August 21, 2026.

The application exercise was launched in December 2025, with the agencies identifying AI and data-centre investment among its objectives.

Facilities selected under the programme must achieve a Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) of 1.25 or better at full IT load. Applicants must also use equipment that meets or exceeds the energy-efficiency requirements in Singapore Standard SS 715:2025 and optimise equipment utilisation. At least 50% of the proposed new data-centre capacity must be powered through eligible green-energy pathways.

SS 715:2025 sets energy-efficiency requirements for data-centre IT equipment and requires covered equipment to operate safely at temperatures of up to 35°C. It sits alongside SS 697:2023, which covers operating data centres at higher temperatures in tropical conditions.

SS 726 extends that standards framework to liquid-cooling infrastructure, covering systems that remove heat directly from higher-density processors.

Singapore’s Energy Market Authority (EMA) expects peak electricity demand to increase by between 2.4% and 4.8% annually over the next decade, reaching between 9.6GW and 11.4GW by 2031. EMA identified energy-intensive sectors including data centres and semiconductor manufacturing among the contributors to demand growth.

The authority has also awarded Tuas Power the right to build 670MW of additional generation capacity, scheduled to enter operation by December 2031.

SS 726 complements Singapore’s Green Data Centre Roadmap, which IMDA introduced in 2024. The roadmap included plans to develop standards for IT equipment efficiency and liquid cooling.

stories.title: AI Boosts Data Center Cooling, Operations Efficiency
stories.summary: Data center operators are increasingly deploying artificial intelligence (AI) to enhance facility efficiency, particularly in cooling and power optimization. This shift is improving energy use, uptime, and incident response times, with major players like Digital Realty and AWS leading the adoption.
stories.content:
Data center operators are increasingly deploying artificial intelligence (AI) to enhance facility efficiency, particularly in cooling and power optimization. This shift is improving energy use, uptime, and incident response times, with major players like Digital Realty and AWS leading the adoption.

Highlights

Digital Realty uses its OPDaaS platform and generative AI for cooling optimization, saving 17,800 MWh in 2025.

AWS deploys generative AI to reduce stranded power and uses AI agents for rapid network incident response.

Schneider Electric leverages AI in digital twins for power/cooling and EcoStruxure IT for predictive maintenance.

IT and OT data convergence is emerging, enabling AI to make more holistic, efficient operational decisions.

Data center operators are increasingly deploying artificial intelligence (AI) to manage their facilities more efficiently, moving AI from pilot to production for tasks ranging from cooling and power optimization to predictive maintenance and incident response. While full autonomy remains rare, AI is delivering measurable gains in energy use, uptime, and operational speed, according to industry analysts.Hyperscalers and large colocation providers are at the forefront, often developing in-house tools. Midsized operators are piloting targeted use cases due to mounting operational pressures, while many smaller environments are still evaluating adoption, according to Roy Illsley, Omdia’s chief analyst for IT operations.

Digital Realty's AI-driven Optimisation

Digital Realty has been applying machine learning for over five years and generative AI for three to four years across its more than 300 global data centers. Chris Sharp, the company’s CTO, highlighted the Operational Data as a Service (OPDaaS) platform, an in-house suite of AI tools that collects sub-second telemetry from power, cooling, and other building systems.This platform uses AI to detect issues like clogged air-cooled system filters, with proactive maintenance leading to double-digit percentage efficiency gains. Digital Realty is also deploying Phaidra’s AI platform at its IAD51 data center in Northern Virginia, which hosts Nvidia, to optimize liquid cooling based on actual compute demand. The company saved 17,800 MWh in 2025 and plans to deploy OPDaaS in 30 more data centers by the end of 2026.

AWS Leverages AI for Network and Power

Amazon Web Services (AWS) uses generative AI to optimize server placement in racks, reducing stranded power—unused available energy. Zak Islam, AWS’s director of network observability and automation, stated that AI agents are also used across network operations to manage infrastructure at scale, investigating and correlating data to identify root causes of network issues in seconds.For routine operational problems, AI reviews incoming tickets, compares them with historical patterns, and often resolves issues without human intervention. AWS also uses AI to monitor its fiber-optic infrastructure, automatically contacting vendors to expedite repairs, and assists engineers with natural language queries for network telemetry data.

DPR Construction and Schneider Electric Deployments

DPR Construction, a national contractor, uses AI for data analytics in pre-construction, drawing on past build data to predict staffing needs, project duration, and sequencing for new data centers. Max Lares, a DPR project executive, noted that the company also pilots robots for overnight site monitoring, improving progress tracking and image quality for clients.Schneider Electric integrates AI into its products and internal operations. Its ETAP electrical power system modeling software and AVEVA industrial operations software, with Nvidia technology, enable the creation of digital twins for power and cooling infrastructure. Steven Carlini, Schneider Electric’s chief advocate for data centers and AI, noted that the company’s EcoStruxure IT software uses AI for remote diagnostics and predictive maintenance, with human oversight for final decisions.

IT/OT Convergence and Autonomy

While AI is more mature on the IT side of data centers, particularly with AIOps tools, the operational technology (OT) side, covering power distribution and cooling, is catching up. Vendors like Schneider Electric and Siemens are incorporating AI into data center infrastructure management (DCIM) systems to monitor and diagnose anomalies in power and cooling, Illsley noted.The next step involves converging IT and OT data into a shared layer, allowing AI to make more holistic decisions. Zoe Roth, senior research analyst at 451 Research, highlighted startups like Phaidra that orchestrate cooling and thermal optimization by streaming telemetry from both IT and building management systems. Despite advancements, fully autonomous data centers remain a remote possibility due to trust issues, with humans likely to remain in the loop for the foreseeable future, according to Dan Thompson, research director at 451 Research.

stories.title: Asia's Connectivity Market Sees Subsea Cable Boom, Power Constraints
stories.summary: Asia's connectivity market is being reshaped by a record wave of subsea cable construction alongside tightening power availability for data centers, according to industry analysis covering markets including India. Together these forces are redirecting digital infrastructure investment and operating strategies across the region.
stories.why_it_matters: Cable landings and power access are becoming the twin determinants of where data center capacity gets built in Asia, favoring markets that can offer both. Investors and operators that misjudge either constraint risk stranded assets as AI-era traffic and compute demand concentrate in fewer, better-resourced hubs.
stories.content:
Asia's connectivity market is undergoing significant shifts, driven by a record wave of subsea cable construction and the escalating importance of power availability for data center expansion. These trends are reshaping digital infrastructure investment and operational strategies across the region, including India.

Highlights

Approximately 40 new subsea cables expected in 2026, with $6 billion investment, marking a decade-high jump.

Power availability now critical constraint for APAC data center growth, surpassing land and fibre access.

AI compute demands are fundamentally reshaping network architecture, increasing capacity and resilience needs.

DayOne Data Centers raised over $2 billion, Vantage Data Centers secured $1.6 billion for Southeast Asia expansion.

The Asian connectivity market is experiencing a rapid transformation, marked by a substantial increase in subsea cable deployments and a fundamental shift where power availability now dictates the growth trajectory of digital infrastructure. This evolution is particularly relevant for data center operators, hyperscalers, and investors in India and the broader Asia-Pacific (APAC) region.

Subsea Capacity Surge and Resilience Focus

A year after concerns about subsea supply scarcity, roughly 40 new cables are projected to enter commercial service in 2026, representing approximately $6 billion in new investment. This marks the largest annual jump in over a decade, with Google alone deploying eight new Pacific systems this year. Notably, a Microsoft- and Lightstorm-backed cable linking India, Malaysia, and Singapore highlights a trend towards hyperscaler-led private systems over traditional carrier-owned consortia. The critical question for 2026 is no longer about sufficient capacity, but ensuring resilience and diversity to mitigate risks from disruptions such as the Red Sea events and the concentration of traffic on a few critical routes and hubs.

Power Availability: The New Constraint

Power availability has emerged as the primary binding constraint for data center growth across APAC, surpassing land and fibre access. Moody's forecasts approximately $800 billion in data center investment in the region by 2030, which could more than double installed capacity. Concurrently, Deloitte projects regional electricity demand from data centers could increase fivefold by the mid-2030s. Operators are adapting by integrating power procurement, including behind-the-meter generation and renewable power purchase agreements (PPAs), into core infrastructure strategy rather than treating it as a secondary consideration.

AI Reshapes Connectivity Architecture

The proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) training, inference, and sovereign compute across Asia is fundamentally altering network architecture. Networks must now support larger data center clusters, heavier workloads, and deliver enhanced capacity, resilience, and programmability. This demand is leading to a re-evaluation of where network capacity is needed next to support the evolving AI ecosystem.

NaaS and Network Automation Advancements

Network-as-a-Service (NaaS) is progressing towards a cloud-like consumption model for connectivity, with platforms like BT's Global Fabric now handling customer traffic. While enterprises seek cloud-like control, industry-wide interoperability and standardised application programming interfaces (APIs) remain areas for further development. Concurrently, AI is moving from pilot to production within live telecom networks, optimising energy and automating operations, thereby doing substantive work rather than being tested in isolation.

Data Sovereignty Intensifies

Data sovereignty regulations are intensifying across the region, with fragmented rules from Vietnam's draft personal data protection law to amendments in Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA). Nearly 90% of APAC enterprises manage multi-cloud workloads that must align with these regulations. This trend is accelerating the evolution of cloud services, positioning them as critical national infrastructure, with telecom operators increasingly becoming key anchors for sovereign AI buildouts in markets not yet served by hyperscalers.

Capital Flowing into Southeast Asia

Capital investment into Southeast Asia's digital infrastructure is accelerating, albeit with increased selectivity regarding power availability and execution risk. DayOne Data Centers secured over $2 billion in equity in January 2026 for expansion into the SIJORI corridor (Singapore, Johor, Batam), Thailand, Japan, and Hong Kong. Similarly, Vantage Data Centers closed a $1.6 billion APAC investment, including a 300MW campus in Johor. This indicates a broader investment trend beyond Singapore into markets like Malaysia, Thailand, and Indonesia, with Malaysia positioning itself as a digital infrastructure gateway to ASEAN.

South Korean telecommunications major SK Telecom has announced the launch of SK Horizon, a new artificial intelligence data center (AI DC) company, which will operate and expand its existing AI DC infrastructure. The move is supported by a combined KRW 3.08 trillion (~ US$ 2.2 billion) equity investment from funds managed by KKR, a global investment firm, and the IMM Investment-Stonebridge consortium.SK Telecom will retain management control of SK Horizon with a 51 percent stake, while KKR and the IMM consortium will hold 29 percent and 20 percent stakes, respectively. This governance restructuring is intended to strengthen expertise and accelerate execution in the AI DC business, according to Kim Seong-soo, CEO of SK Broadband, who is expected to concurrently serve as CEO of SK Horizon.

Capacity Expansion and Infrastructure Focus

SK Horizon's mandate includes expanding its infrastructure to a total capacity of 318 MW, encompassing eight data centers already in operation across locations like Seocho, Ilsan, Bundang, Gasan, Centum, Yangju, and Pangyo. New AI DCs currently under construction, including those in Ulsan and Guro, will also fall under its purview. The company will also focus on the phased expansion of its submarine cable infrastructure, which is deemed essential for global AI businesses.The establishment of SK Horizon, alongside SK Hyper, a recently formed specialized company targeting 5 GW of capacity by 2029 and 15 GW by 2035 for new AI DC projects, completes SKT's full-scale AI DC business structure. SK Telecom expects this streamlined decision-making to enhance funding efforts for key business areas, including through external investment.

Investor Perspective

Keith Kim, Partner at KKR, stated that Korea's advanced digital ecosystem and growing demand for AI capacity provide a strong foundation for SK Horizon's growth. KKR is making this investment primarily from its Asia Pacific infrastructure strategy, adding to its over USD 100 billion in infrastructure assets under management globally.Kim Byung-hun, Head of Infrastructure at IMM Investment, highlighted the importance of AI data centers and submarine cables for Korea's digital sovereignty and industrial competitiveness. The IMM Investment-Stonebridge Consortium, comprising IMM Investment and Stonebridge Capital, aims to build a sustainable growth structure by combining global and domestic capital strength.

Yotta Data Services is in the process of ordering 50,000 Nvidia Vera Rubin graphics processing units (GPUs) and an additional 45,000 GB-300 GPUs, which are part of Nvidia’s Blackwell family architecture and represent the company’s latest offerings. This procurement, estimated at around $7.5 billion for the Vera Rubin chips, networking, and associated equipment, will be the largest GPU order in India to date, according to Yotta Data Services Cofounder, Managing Director (MD), and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Sunil Gupta.An additional $750 million will be required for the construction of the data center infrastructure. AI Compute Capacity Boost

The Vera Rubin GPUs are designed for agentic artificial intelligence (AI), enabling advanced models to utilise tools and execute complex, multi-step problem-solving. These next-generation GPUs offer 10x higher efficiency than the previous Blackwell architecture, delivering 5x faster inference and 3.5x improved training capabilities. The graphic chips use a 3 nanometre manufacturing process, enhancing data memory speeds beyond 1,500 terabytes per second and significantly lowering the cost per token.Previously, Hyderabad-based AMI Intelligence, part of the Greenko group, had placed a binding order for 9,000 Vera Rubin GPUs for its intelligent factory in Hyderabad. Yotta’s current order, once finalised, will surpass this, establishing a new benchmark for AI compute investment in India.

KUALA LUMPUR (Aug 28): Kerjaya Prospek Group Bhd (KL:KERJAYA) plans to maintain its 31% stake in ES Sunlogy Bhd (KL:SUNLOGY), with the aim of tapping the company’s expertise in semiconductor, data centre and power-grid projects.

Kerjaya Prospek became ES Sunlogy’s largest shareholder after three acquisitions between July 16 and Aug 17, investing a total of RM64.3 million.

Its chairman Datuk Seri Tee Eng Ho told reporters at the group's second-quarter earnings briefing on Friday that the group intends to keep the 31% stake for now. Kerjaya Prospek has worked with ES Sunlogy for about 10 years, with the latter serving as one of its subcontractors.

ES Sunlogy, which listed on Bursa Malaysia’s ACE Market in February 2025, provides high- and low-voltage electrical systems, extra-low-voltage systems, mechanical engineering services and solar energy solutions.

Despite recent domestic political uncertainty, Tee said Kerjaya Prospek had not seen any impact on its construction tendering activities and orderbook replenishment.

“No, so far no. Business is still going,” he said when asked whether domestic political uncertainty could delay construction tenders.

On its construction business, Kerjaya Prospek expressed confidence to clinch more than RM3 billion in new orders for FY2026, having secured about RM2.37 billion in new jobs so far this year.

Kerjaya Prospek had an outstanding construction order book of about RM5 billion as at end-June this year, of which around 58% or RM2.9 billion comprised related-party projects.

On rising operating costs, including raw materials such as copper and cement, Tee said the group's strategy is to work harder and secure new jobs with higher margins.

Copper prices have risen about 16% this year so far. Copper was at about US$12,504 per tonne at end-2025, before rising to its peak of US$14,850 on Aug 17. It was traded at US$14,490 on Aug 27.

Kerjaya Prospek on Friday (Aug 28) reported a 22.6% year-on-year increase in second-quarter profit to RM66.67 million, despite revenue falling 25.3% to RM403.09 million.

The group attributed the earnings improvement mainly to prudent cost management and contributions from higher-margin projects. Its net profit margin improved to 16.54% in 2QFY2026 from 10.1% a year earlier.

For the first half of FY2026 (1HFY2026), its net profit rose 23% to RM 124 million from RM100.5 million a year ago, while revenue dropped 16% to RM849.9 million from RM1.01 billion.

stories.title: Data Centres, Cloud Projects Make Up Nearly Half of Malaysia's RM218.5b Approved Investments in 1H2026 — Mida
stories.summary: Malaysia's approved investments reached RM218.5 billion in the first half of 2026, up 11.7% year-on-year, with data center and cloud-computing projects accounting for nearly half of the total, according to MIDA.
stories.why_it_matters: The figures confirm Malaysia's emergence as one of APAC's primary data center destinations, with digital infrastructure now dominating the national investment pipeline. That concentration raises both the stakes for power and land policy and the risk of overexposure if hyperscale demand cools.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Aug 28): Data centre and cloud-computing projects accounted for nearly half of Malaysia's approved investments in the first half of 2026 (1H2026), as overall approved investments rose 11.7% year-on-year to RM218.5 billion.

Data centre and cloud-computing projects attracted RM95.8 billion in investments during the six-month period, equivalent to nearly 44% of total approved investments, as demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing power continued to grow across the region, the Malaysian Investment Development Authority (Mida) said in a statement on Friday.

The services sector accounted for the bulk of approved investments at RM149.6 billion or 68.5% of the total, followed by manufacturing at RM51.3 billion or 23.5%, and the primary sector at RM17.6 billion or 8%.

Within services, approved investments rose 21% year-on-year, while information and communications — which includes data centre and cloud-computing projects — surged 68.2% to RM103.3 billion.

Foreign investments rose 18.5% to RM126.9 billion and accounted for 58.1% of total approved investments, while domestic investments increased 3.5% to RM91.6 billion.

The US was the largest source of foreign investments at RM33.1 billion, followed by Singapore at RM25.9 billion, Japan at RM22.3 billion, China at RM16.5 billion and the Cayman Islands at RM4.1 billion. These five top foreign sources of investment accounted for more than 80% of approved foreign investments.

By location, Selangor attracted the most approved investments at RM70 billion across 835 projects, followed by Johor at RM59.4 billion, Kuala Lumpur at RM26.6 billion, Penang at RM20.2 billion and Sarawak at RM10.8 billion.

Mida chairman Tengku Datuk Seri Zafrul Abdul Aziz said the manufacturing sector saw semiconductor investment shift from back-end assembly towards front-end design and equipment, reflecting the implementation of the National Semiconductor Strategy.

"Guided by the New Industrial Master Plan 2030, Mida will continue to prioritise and implement investments that transfer technology, deepen local vendor participation and create high-value jobs for Malaysians,” he said.

Approved manufacturing investments, however, fell 25.1% year-on-year to RM51.3 billion, although the number of projects surged 88.2% to 973.

Mida said the decline was due to unusually large investments of RM18.5 billion in basic metals, chemicals and non-metallic minerals approved in the first half of 2025. Excluding these projects, manufacturing investments would have grown 2.6%.

Domestic manufacturing investments rose 23% to RM18.6 billion, while foreign investments accounted for RM32.7 billion or 63.8% of manufacturing approvals.

Meanwhile, approved investments in the primary sector surged more than fivefold to RM17.6 billion from RM3.5 billion, driven entirely by 23 offshore oil and gas projects.

The first-half figure has already surpassed the RM14.2 billion approved for the primary sector for the whole of 2025.

Looking ahead, Mida said it was reviewing 227 investment proposals worth RM72.1 billion as at Aug 10, comprising 128 services projects worth RM36.5 billion and 99 manufacturing projects worth RM35.6 billion.

Another RM58.4 billion worth of potential investments were under discussion, with the near-term pipeline concentrated in semiconductors, AI infrastructure, renewable energy and medical devices.

On the implementation of previously approved investments, Mida said 87% of the 5,822 manufacturing projects approved between 2021 and June 2026 had reached implementation stage, while 9.8% remained in the planning phase and 3.2% were not implemented.

More than 90% of manufacturing projects approved between 2021 and 2024 have been implemented, while the implementation rates for projects approved in 2025 and 1H2026 stood at 83.8% and 65.5%, respectively.

Mida chief executive officer Datuk Sikh Shamsul Ibrahim Sikh Abdul Majid said securing investment commitments was only part of Mida's role, as the agency also helps investors overcome regulatory and implementation hurdles to ensure approved projects materialise.

"Our engagement does not end at approvals: we stay involved to handhold projects and, through #InvestLokal, deepen the participation of SMEs and local vendors, so that each ringgit committed becomes real capacity and skilled employment for Malaysians,” he said.

stories.title: SoftBank Seeks Another US$10b Loan for OpenAI Stake Funding
stories.summary: SoftBank Group Corp is seeking a US$10 billion (RM40.3 billion) loan, as it looks for more funding to help refinance debt used for its investment in US tech giant OpenAI, according to people familiar with the matter.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
(Aug 28): SoftBank Group Corp is seeking a US$10 billion (RM40.3 billion) loan, as it looks for more funding to help refinance debt used for its investment in US tech giant OpenAI, according to people familiar with the matter.

The interest margin on the two-year facility would be around 275 basis point over the benchmark Secured Overnight Financing Rate, and Mizuho Bank Ltd is the mandated lead arranger and bookrunner, said the people, who asked not to be identified as the matter is private.

The loan would add to SoftBank’s flurry of recent debt financing activities tied to its bet on OpenAI, including a potential bond sale of as much as US$20 billion, despite concerns about growing credit risks in the artificial intelligence sector. SoftBank, founded and led by billionaire Masayoshi Son, is slated to invest close to US$65 billion in OpenAI by October.

Proceeds of the loan could partly be used to repay a US$40 billion bridge loan secured earlier this year for the OpenAI investments, the people said. Commitments are due Aug 31 and banks are already in talks to join, the people added.

The International Financing Review reported news of the deal earlier this week.

SoftBank is also looking at tapping the bond market for additional funding. It’s considering US$10 billion to US$20 billion offering to help refinance the bridge loan, and it’s planning a record ¥1 trillion retail bond sale in its home market for its investment commitments to OpenAI.

The company earlier this month also secured a US$10 billion loan backed by its OpenAI stake, which includes covenants that may require it to post cash or repay early.

SoftBank and Mizuho declined to comment.

SoftBank’s borrowings come as US tech firms are planning to pour trillions of dollars into data centres and other AI infrastructure in the coming years. Companies have already borrowed more than US$410 billion so far this year for such facilities and other AI investments in the bond markets alone, according to data compiled by *Bloomberg News*.

stories.title: Gamuda Lands Another RM3.57 Bil in Hyperscale Data Centre Jobs in Port Dickson
stories.summary: Gamuda Bhd has won contracts worth a combined RM3.57 billion to construct two hyperscale data centers in Port Dickson, Negeri Sembilan, extending its run of large digital infrastructure wins.
stories.why_it_matters: The awards spread Malaysia's data center growth beyond the established Johor and Klang Valley hubs, opening a new development corridor in Negeri Sembilan. For Gamuda, the contracts cement its transformation from a traditional builder into a major beneficiary of the hyperscale construction boom.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Aug 28): Gamuda Bhd (KL:GAMUDA) on Friday said it has secured contracts worth a combined RM3.57 billion to build two hyperscale data centres in Port Dickson, Negeri Sembilan.

In a filing with Bursa Malaysia, the construction giant said the contracts were awarded to its wholly-owned subsidiary Gamuda Engineering Sdn Bhd (GESB) by a US-headquartered multinational technology company.

The scope of works covers the construction of two single-storey hyperscale data centre facilities, including site infrastructure, building core and shell construction, and mechanical, electrical and plumbing (MEP) fit-out works.

The first contract is worth RM1.79 billion, while the second is valued at RM1.78 billion.

Both projects are expected to commence in the fourth quarter of 2026. The first data centre is scheduled for completion in the third quarter of 2028, while the second is expected to be completed in the fourth quarter of 2028.

The latest awards mark Gamuda’s third hyperscale data centre construction job in Port Dickson this year.

The group previously secured a RM1.72 billion contract in April and another RM1.71 billion contract earlier this month for data centre construction in the same location.

As at end-April, Gamuda’s construction order book stood at RM52 billion.

Gamuda said the latest projects are expected to contribute positively to the group’s revenue and earnings for the financial year ending July 31, 2027 and thereafter until their completion.

Gamuda shares fell 11 sen, or 2.4%, to RM4.41 after the announcement, giving the group a market capitalisation of RM26.39 billion. The stock has fallen more than 11% since the start of the year.

stories.title: CXMT's 570% Rally Raises Bar for First Earnings Since IPO
stories.summary: CXMT Corp’s first earnings as a public company will test whether its business can live up to a stock market debut that instantly made it China’s most valuable listed company.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
(Aug 28): CXMT Corp’s first earnings as a public company will test whether its business can live up to a stock market debut that instantly made it China’s most valuable listed company.

Shares of China’s homegrown memory chipmaker have jumped more than 570% since listing and remain within 10% of their peak, making it the most resilient market debut onshore this quarter, data compiled by *Bloomberg* show. They fell as much as 1.7% on Friday.  

As the world’s fourth-biggest DRAM producer, CXMT has become a symbol of China’s effort to reduce its reliance on foreign technology. Even after the surge, the stock still trades at a significant discount to global peers, Goldman Sachs Group Inc said. Closing that gap may depend on whether CXMT can show its profits are sustainable and its capacity expansion can deliver further growth.

“It’s no longer a question of whether CXMT can generate exceptional profits,” said Wang Xi, chairman of Shenzhen-based investment firm Jiuxing Investment Co. “The quality and durability of those numbers, pace of spending, and tangible progress in high-bandwidth — those factors will drive earnings expectations and set its valuation anchor from here.”

Wang said investors are also turning more selective on memory stocks, looking for fresh evidence that validates the company’s business model and growth expectations.

CXMT has forecast a strong first half, expecting revenue of 110 billion yuan (RM65.9 billion) to 120 billion yuan, at least double its first-quarter sales of 50.8 billion yuan, according to its prospectus. Net profit is seen at 50 billion yuan to 57 billion yuan, compared with 24.8 billion yuan in the three months through March. It’s set to report results on Friday.

That guidance helped fuel the stock’s blockbuster debut late July, when CXMT reached a market value of 3.3 trillion yuan. It went on to surpass Hong Kong-listed Tencent Holdings Ltd in the following days, becoming China’s largest listed company by market capitalisation.

There are signs that even blowout earnings may not be enough. SK Hynix Inc shares fell almost 10% after reporting a sixfold surge in quarterly profit. Samsung Electronics Co also declined after a sharp profit increase. Chinese memory firms including GigaDevice Semiconductor Inc and Shenzhen Techwinsemi Technology Co saw similarly muted or negative reactions to results or preliminary figures.

The reactions this week to Chinese hardware tech earnings have been subdued. Sharetronic Data Technology Co traded lower after reporting earnings that more than quadrupled. Victory Giant Technology Co shares fell more than 7% in Hong Kong following a revenue miss.

The “violent AI selloff” in July marked a shift in investor psychology, said Yang Tingwu, a fund manager at Fujian Tongheng Investment. Strong earnings may make a company’s valuation look cheaper, he said, but that is rarely a reason to turn bullish on a cyclical stock. “That’s just the market’s way of signaling peak earnings may be approaching.”

CXMT trades at about 10 times estimated 2027 earnings, a “significant discount to global peers”, according to Goldman Sachs. The multiple is based on forecasts for net income to more than double to 361 billion yuan in 2027 from an estimated 161 billion yuan this year.

Capacity will be central to that outlook. CXMT’s “very aggressive” investment plan will be an important factor as investors gauge the global memory supply-demand balance by 2028, Goldman analysts including Allen Chang wrote this week.

They expect CXMT’s scarcity value, product mix upgrades and role as a beneficiary of supplier diversification to help its earnings outpace the industry, underpinning their Street-high price target of 129 yuan. The shares traded at 58.36 yuan as of mid-day on Friday.

CXMT’s reign at the top of China’s stock market may soon face a new challenger. Yangtze Memory Technologies Co, or YMTC, has joined the IPO pipeline with plans to raise 33 billion yuan on Shanghai’s Star board, more than the 30 billion yuan sought by CXMT.

The Wuhan-based company makes NAND flash memory, the storage technology used in solid-state drives and data centres. Like CXMT, it emerged from China’s state-led drive to reduce dependence on foreign technology and is now the country’s dominant player in the sector. YMTC ranks third globally by sales and output, according to its prospectus, while its net profit and net margin surpassed CXMT’s in the March quarter.

That could make YMTC an even bigger test of investor appetite for China’s memory-chip champions. NAND faces fewer manufacturing barriers, potentially giving YMTC more room to challenge global incumbents.

“Valuations across hardware firms in China are propped up by the idea that self-sufficiency will create a large total addressable market,” said Morningstar Inc analyst Jing Jie Yu. “YMTC will probably start from a stronger competitive position than the rest.”
